8
Two masses, M and m, are connected by an inextensible string which passes over a frictionless
pulley. Mass M rests on a frictionless slope, as shown.

The slope is at an angle  to the horizontal.
The two masses are initially held stationary and then released. Mass M accelerates down the
slope.
Which expression must be correct?

hints: Notice that $M$ accelerates down the frictionless slope while $m$ is pulled upward, so compare the two forces trying to move the string in opposite directions.
Resolve the weight $M g$ parallel to the slope of angle $\theta$. Only the $M g \sin\theta$ component acts down the slope to oppose the weight $m g$ of the hanging mass.
For motion down the slope to start, the downslope component must exceed $m g$. Divide both sides by $M g$ to get a relation between $\sin\theta$ and $m/M$.
walkthrough: Identify the two competing pulls on the inextensible string: the component of $M$'s weight down the slope and the weight $m g$ of the hanging mass pulling up the slope.
The weight $M g$ acts vertically down. Its component parallel to a slope at angle $\theta$ is $M g \sin\theta$ down the slope, while $M g \cos\theta$ acts into the slope.
Because pulley and slope are frictionless, the only thing opposing $M g \sin\theta$ along the direction of motion is the tension, which must support $m$.
Since $M$ accelerates down the slope after release, the resultant force must be down the slope, so $M g \sin\theta$ must be greater than $m g$.
Divide by $M g$: $\sin\theta > m/M$. This is option C.

A.explanation: This reverses the inequality. If $M$ moves down the slope, the downslope pull must be larger than the pull from $m$, not smaller.

B.explanation: The downslope component of weight uses $\sin\theta$, not $\cos\theta$. $M g \cos\theta$ is the component normal to the slope.

C.explanation: Downslope motion requires $M g \sin\theta > m g$, which cancels to $\sin\theta > m/M$.

D.explanation: This uses the wrong trigonometric component. $\cos\theta$ gives the force pressing $M$ into the slope, not the force pulling it down the slope.
